title.title: Prime and polynomial distances in colourings of the plane

editorial_contributions.text:
Summary: We observe that an old theorem of \textit{R. L. Graham} [J. Comb. Theory, Ser. A 28, 89--97 (1980; Zbl 0428.05004)] implies that for any positive integer \(s\), there exists some positive integer \(T(s)\) such that every \(s\)-colouring of \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) contains a monochromatic pair of points \((x,y)\), \((x^\prime,y^\prime)\) with \((x-x^\prime)^2 - (y-y^\prime)^2 = (T(s))^2\). By scaling, this implies that every finite colouring of \(\mathbb{Q}^2\) contains a monochromatic pair of points \((x,y),(x^\prime,y^\prime)\) with \((x-x^\prime)^2 - (y-y^\prime)^2 = 1\), which answers in a strong sense a problem of \textit{O. Kosheleva} and \textit{V. Kreinovich} [Geombinatorics 19, No. 1, 14--17 (2009; Zbl 1507.05035)] on a pseudo-Euclidean analogue of the Hadwiger-Nelson problem.

The proof of Graham's theorem [loc. cit.] relies on repeated applications of van der Waerden's theorem, and so the resulting function \(T(s)\) grows extremely quickly. We give alternative proof in the weaker setting of having a second spatial dimension that results in a significantly improved bound. To be more precise, we prove that for every positive integer \(s\) with \(s\equiv 2 \pmod{4} \), every \(s\)-colouring of \(\mathbb{Z}^3\) contains a monochromatic pair of points \((x,y,z)\), \((x^\prime,y^\prime,z^\prime)\) such that \((x-x^\prime)^2 + (y-y')^2 - (z-z^\prime)^2 = (5^{(s-2)/4}(8\cdot 5^{(s-2)/2})!)^2\). In fact, we prove a stronger density version. The density version in \(\mathbb{Z}^2\) remains open.

editorial_contributions.text:
The chromatic number of the plane (CNP) is the minimum number of colors required to color the plane in such a way that there exists no monochromatic pair of points with distance \(1\). The problem was posed around 1950 and the early work on CNP showed that the chromatic number is between \(4\) and \(7\). The lower bound is due to the Moser Spindle graph, a \(7\)-vertex unit-distance (UD) graph with \(11\) edges. In a UD graph, the vertices are points in the plane and they are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is exactly \(1\). The upper bound can be shown by a tessellation of the plane using hexagon tiles for which the maximum distance within a tile is slightly smaller than \(1\). Each tile has a single color and tiles of the same color can be placed more than distance \(1\) from each other.

\textit{A. D. N. J. de Grey} [Geombinatorics 28, No. 1, 18--31 (2018; Zbl 1404.05063)] improved the lower bound of CNP by constructing a 1581-vertex UD graph with chromatic number \(5\). Several interestig results followed but existing techniques appear insufficient to construct unit-distance graphs with chromatic number \(6\), if they exists. Important insights might come from odd-distance (OD) graphs, in which two points are connected by an edge whenever the distance between them is odd. To encourage research in this direction, the authors pose the challenge of constructing an odd-distance graph of chromatic number \(6\) or proving that it doesn't exist. Furthermore, a \(5\)-chromatic unit-distance graph of 1441 vertices without Moser Spindles is presented.

editorial_contributions.text: Summary: The upper (lower) chromatic number \(\Bar\chi(H)\) of a mixed hypergraph \(H=(X,C,D)\) is the maximum (minimum) number of colors that can be assigned to the vertices of \(H\) in such a way that each \(C\)-edge contains a monochromatic pair of vertices and each \(D\)-edge has two vertices colored differently. The upper (lower) chromatic number of a mixed hypergraph is closely related to the number of edges, and the number of edges is closely related to the connectness of the pair graphs of its vertices. The relationship between the coloring and the connectness of the pair graphs of its vertices of a \(C\)-hypergraph is discussed, and it is proved that for any positive integer \(n(\geq3)\), there exists a 3-uniform \(C\)-hypergraph with upper chromatic number \(n\) and minimum connected pair graphs.
